The convergent evidence linking radiation-induced p21- and p16-positive senescent cell accumulation to progressive bone loss, impaired osteogenesis, and vascular failure directly parallels the pathophysiology targeted by D + Q in preclinical bone models. Senomorphic strategies, particularly JAK/STAT inhibition, represent a complementary rather than competing approach, and may be especially relevant in the ORN context where complete senescent cell clearance may not be achievable in chronically irradiated tissue. Immune-mediated clearance, epigenetic reprogramming, and mitochondrial redox strategies remain earlier in development and require substantially more mechanistic work before their ORN relevance can be assessed. Of all the platforms discussed, biomaterial-assisted local delivery of senolytics (i.e., bone-targeted or injectable scaffold-based systems) represents the most translatable near-term strategy, as it addresses both the pharmacokinetic limitations of systemic senolytic administration and the localized nature of mandibular ORN pathology.

The regenerative strategies discussed in this review are summarized in Table 5, spanning approaches from proof-of-concept in vitro irradiated cell models to early human feasibility reports. Across these studies, the therapeutic focus has expanded from replacement of radiation-damaged cells and passive structural support toward restoration of endogenous cellular function and active modification of the irradiated microenvironment.

ORN remains a major clinical challenge due to its complex, multiscale pathophysiology and its combined detrimental effects on bone, vasculature, immune function, and overlying soft tissues. While RT remains a cornerstone of HNC treatment, the resulting long-term tissue damage underscores the need for therapeutic strategies that address not only structural loss but also persistent biological dysfunction within irradiated tissues. Despite the encouraging preclinical evidence discussed in this article, none of the completed studies directly evaluated senolytic or senomorphic therapy in a mandibular ORN model or in ORN patients. Most animal studies used a single high radiation dose directed toward the femur or lower limb and initiated treatment immediately after irradiation. ORN, in contrast, commonly develops months or years after fractionated HNC RT and involves a complex interaction among cellular senescence, vascular injury, fibrosis, mucosal breakdown, microbial exposure, mechanical trauma, and impaired immune function.

While senotherapeutic agents are promising, they are not specifically approved by the FDA for clinical use to target senescent cells. Although animal studies show strong results and early human trials suggest short-term functional benefits, important questions about proper dosing and off-target cytotoxicity remain unanswered. Future studies should therefore evaluate senotherapeutics in clinically relevant mandibular models using fractionated radiation schedules and delayed treatment after senescence has become established. Outcomes should include not only microCT and senescence markers but also mandibular vascularity, fibrosis, osteocyte viability, mucosal healing, infection, mechanical integrity, bone remodeling, and functional regeneration. Studies should also determine whether senolytic treatment interferes with tumor control or removes senescent cells involved in wound repair and immune surveillance.

Beyond efficacy, the clinical translation of senotherapeutic-biomaterial combination strategies faces substantial regulatory and manufacturing hurdles. Constructs that combine a biomaterial scaffold with senolytics, growth factors, cells, or EVs are likely to be classified as combination products by the FDA, requiring coordination across device, biologic, and drug regulatory frameworks depending on the primary mode of action. This classification complexity increases development timelines and costs, and demands early engagement with regulatory agencies to define the appropriate approval pathway. Manufacturing presents additional challenges: cell- and EV-loaded biomaterials require reproducible, scalable production under good manufacturing practice (GMP) conditions, with rigorous quality control of cell source, passage number, loading efficiency, and release kinetics [138]. Cryopreservation and shelf-life limitations further complicate clinical deployment [185]. For senolytic small molecules, pharmacokinetic challenges including low bioavailability, rapid systemic clearance, and off-target cytotoxicity must be addressed through formulation strategies such as bone-targeted liposomes or controlled-release scaffolds before clinical translation is feasible [236,237]. Taken together, these barriers underscore the need for early-phase clinical trials designed specifically for ORN that incorporate rigorous safety monitoring, standardized outcome measures, and mechanistic endpoints alongside functional assessments.

Future efforts in ORN management should therefore prioritize integrated combination strategies that unite senescence-targeting interventions with bone tissue engineering approaches. Localized delivery of senolytic or senomorphic agents using biomaterial scaffolds or controlled-release systems may allow precise targeting of pathological senescent cell populations while minimizing systemic toxicity. When combined with stem cells, osteoinductive factors, or angiogenic cues, such approaches have the potential to both remove barriers to healing and actively promote restoration of healthy tissue architecture and function.

In summary, the future of ORN treatment lies in interdisciplinary, mechanism-driven approaches that address both the causes and consequences of radiation-induced tissue injury. By integrating senotherapeutic strategies with regenerative medicine, it may be possible to move beyond symptomatic management toward durable biological resolution of ORN, improving functional outcomes and quality of life for patients undergoing RT for HNC.

ORN should no longer be seen solely as an inexorable consequence of structural tissue destruction, but rather as a pathological state perpetuated by a maladaptive irradiated microenvironment. This conceptual shift reframes treatment from the mere replacement of necrotic tissue toward the restoration of regenerative competence. The integration of senescence-targeted interventions with biomaterial, cellular, and molecular regenerative platforms may therefore represent the most cogent path toward durable recovery by concurrently dismantling the biological impediments to healing and reinstating the mechanisms required for functional bone regeneration.

figures.caption: Hallmarks and therapeutic targeting of cellular senescence.
